newsitem.title: UK: Options-Calls dominate as coffee futures shine.
newsitem.headline: Options-Calls dominate as coffee futures shine.

text.p: Strategies moved in opposite direction in soft options this week with bullish coffee players turning to calls as the futures market became volatile.
But cocoa buyers continued to adopt a bearish stance at what is seen as a relatively cheap premium, while some traders rolled expiring December puts forward to March and May.
Coffee volatilities have risen on the back of fluctuating London and New York markets.
"There's very little open interest in options," said a trader. "Calls dominate as people are taking a bullish view of the market," he said.
There have been some buying near-the-money and out-of-the-money calls in January. Buying in coffee calls centred around the January $1,400 and $1,450 strike.
Volatilities were traded up to 43-44 percent on Thursday on the calls. "It's a good buy at around 30 percent, about two or three percent higher than last week," another said.
Options volume reached 2,366 lots for the week beginning October 31.
Coffee futures rebounded to trade at a high of $1,476 a tonne basis January on Thursday after being trapped at the $1,375-$1,410 range for the past weeks.
The rise followed steep gains in New York futures as funds switched to commodities after equities and bonds eased.
But London pulled back slightly to hover at around $1,440 by mid-morning on Friday.
Option traders said a good strategy was to do a ratio put spread, buying January $1,500 put and sell $1,450.
In cocoa, some traders rolled forward the December 950 stg put strike into the distant May 925 stg put ahead of the December expiry on November 20.
Cocoa options were active on Thursday with 1,150 lots traded following large two-way put spread deals.
December/May 950 put spread was traded at 12 premium to the May 950 put.
"It looks as if the buyer was rolling an existing short forward to May," said trade house Sucden in a daily commentary.
"The seller of the December was effectively going long the December-May switch using the options spread," it said.
The forward May call traded lightly at an implied volatility of around 18 percent. "In our view this is a long term buy than sell," Sucden said.
Options premiums in London are relatively a bargain and traders said any offers of around 20 percent or lower even on the forward positions can be considered as a buy.
Ccooa futures remained under selling presure but range-bound this week ahead of a seasonal production rise.
Arrivals from Ivory Coast are expected to gain momentum in the coming weeks.
Traders expect little market movement until a clearer 1996/97 crop picture emerges.
Early assessments put a world cocoa deficit of between 150,000 and 200,000 tonnes in the current crop year.
